title: Qt: Display extcap uncheckable multicheck items as labels
description: Commit e1a8f0119ebb ("Extcap prefs: Editor remembers empty values") inadvertently made the immutable checkbox visible next to uncheckable multicheck items. Restore former behavior, that is display only labels for uncheckable multicheck items, by setting unchecked state only for checkable items.

added 2 commits

  • 78e70dd4 - Qt: Do not display uncheckable items checkboxes
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/9091/diffs?diff_id=556559134&start_sha=0b258aa51ccee8f25380b7bbe3653014213e2086)

That is actually bad UI design. Even if you are not able to interact with the checkbox, an UI element should NEVER present itself differently depending on a given situation. So, if this is a checkbox, it should always present as such, even if in the given scenario it cannot be interacted with. Having the item displayed as a label will give the user pause the next time when it is presented as a checkbox.

Remember, most interactions with UI are instinctive and therefore scenarios should never change or otherwise the user will simply not see the checkbox or register it properly.

The original reason why multiselect was added (back in GTK UI) was to allow labels to be below the checkboxes. The uncheckable items were always considered to be just additional information, to be displayed under the checkbox and never intended to be displayed as checkbox itself.

I don't know when it changed, but I am fairly certain that in some Qt version there were no checkboxes next to uncheckable items.

I think presenting something that user cannot ever enable/disable as "unchecked" is really counter-intuitive.

Please see attached screenshots for the real reason why I implemented uncheckable items in multicheck extcap configuration. The label only option (i.e. uncheckable items) was there since the very first time the multicheck was committed to SVN repository.

Please tell me, how the user can tell here that the items without address in square brackets are not checkable and there is absolutely nothing that the user can do about it.

![UncheckableCheckboxes](/uploads/b9b3b3d9eb0ea34b70dec647dbdfe8a6/UncheckableCheckboxes.png)

It is perfectly clear in my opinion if the checkbox is not displayed next to uncheckable items and thus if these are presented as simple labels.

![UncheckableLabels](/uploads/81fc25165580ca0954fefefe0c615739/UncheckableLabels.png)

The labels are really important as otherwise guessing what is the "USB composite device" is not helpful at all. The actual tree structure (and labels) is coming directly from Windows. It is not easy to "pick just one thing" to display, therefore the full tree was made available to allow the user to determine what devices are connected (and the capture can be started from, without requiring the user to only capture from newly connected devices as there are USB devices that cannot be physically detached, e.g. most laptop cameras).

So you are saying, that those will always be labels and never be checkable? If so, I see your point and agree, that removing the checkbox would be a good thing. But in this case, the distinction is not going far enough. I would additionally try to change the appearance further e.g. by making the text of the uncheckable items italic or bold to better indicate that they are simply there as a helping device not to be checked ever. 

I also See your point, that the current implementation is somewhat a misfit for the whole thing. It kind of seems as we would need a completely different kind of selection type, where it can be better distinguished between the informational parts and the active parts. Would you agree?

Yes, the Non-clickable items were always intended to be just labels and never be checkable. Turns out I was wrong about the SVN, it was already after Wireshark has started using gerrit. The parent parameter to multicheck was added in 9c1225f73511b59dd74273545fac401d711cea36 and the original mailing list discussion about it is at https://www.wireshark.org/lists/wireshark-dev/201409/msg00065.html

I don't think another kind of selector is needed. The non-clickable checkbox was not there in Wireshark 3.3.0 as can be seen on slide 15 of USB Analysis 101 from Sharkfest'20 Virtual https://sharkfestvirtual.wireshark.org/assets/presentations20/14.zip

All this change does is just brings back the way it used to work and this is all that is needed.

Actually, there was no checkbox next to uncheckable items until e1a8f0119ebb331ffc843553f15be0fda288b809, so the behavior was changed not so long time ago. Also the reason for the change seems to be definitely related to handling checkable items (uncheckable item state cannot be changed).

> Yes, the Non-clickable items were always intended to be just labels

I.e., that part of the dialog is an set of information about the interface, rather than a set of capture options for the interface.

> I.e., that part of the dialog is an set of information about the interface, rather than a set of capture options for the interface.

I find it hard to interpret what you mean. Do you mean that it is fine if non-clickable items are displayed as labels? Or do you mean that the whole idea was wrong from the beginning?

I think that nobody really wanted the "non-checkable checkboxes" to be visible and this MR really fixes unintended consequences of e1a8f0119ebb331ffc843553f15be0fda288b809.

> Do you mean that it is fine if non-clickable items are displayed as labels?

Yes.

I was also guessing that some of the confusion about this might have stemmed from an inference that those items were, as they were in an options dialog, options, rather than just information, and was attempting to clarify that.

> Or do you mean that the whole idea was wrong from the beginning?

No.

It *does* raise the question of whether that information should go in the options dialog or in some other place in the UI, so that people who want that information don't have to guess that it's in the options dialog.

Just going from this conversation it becomes more and more clear to me, that the way we present this information is just plain confusing. I absolutely get, that it is important information and therefore should be displayed, but for me it is much rather a descriptive text for a selected option, than something that should be inside the tree.

So, maybe not a completely new element, but we could think of adding this information into a description box right beside or underneath the selector, which can change the context whenever a new item is selected and is being hidden completely, if no element within the tree has any item description.

That would be a change to multiselect, but one that would a. improve understanding of the presented information as well as correlation and b. be a real added benefit for the end-user.

@rknall Could you please post a mockup because the way I understand what you wrote is both going to be non-trivial to implement and really annoying to use. I might be completely misunderstanding what you wrote, but I believe the screenshots, like I posted at https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/9091#note_1208201696 are really valuable when discussing such issues.

However, despite this being not ideal, I believe this MR should be merged as it just restores the old behavior (plain label) that was inadvertently changed earlier this year **and** the uncheckable checkbox is really much more confusing than a plain label.

commits_data.title: Qt: Display extcap uncheckable multicheck items as labels
commits_data.message:
Qt: Display extcap uncheckable multicheck items as labels

Commit e1a8f0119ebb ("Extcap prefs: Editor remembers empty values")
inadvertently made the immutable checkbox visible next to uncheckable
multicheck items. Restore former behavior, that is display only labels
for uncheckable multicheck items, by setting unchecked state only for
checkable items.

Uncheckable items, since its introduction in commit 9c1225f73511
("Modify multicheck to accept parent parameter."), were used to display
additional labels in USBPcap configuration options to aid user in
determining which individual device to filter on. Without the additional
information determining for example which "USB composite device" is of
interest to the user is really problematic.
